periods.activity_title: Who Carries Words? Pre-Reading and First Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.203): paired discussion — postal profession, challenges, impact on people
Reflect and Respond (p.203): group discussion — carrying words, carriers, means of connection

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a brief look at the pictures in Reflect and Respond (p.203) and invites students to name the profession shown. Pairs discuss the three oral prompts — profession, difficulties, impact on those they meet — and one or two pairs share aloud.

Groups of four take up the second Reflect and Respond set (p.203): how words can be 'carried', who could carry them, and what means people use to stay connected. Teacher draws out responses and connects the title 'Carrier of Words' to the discussion.

Teacher reads the prose aloud from p.203 to p.207, students following in their textbooks. Teacher pauses at significant moments — the description of Khetaram's slumped shoulder and the desert distances — to let the imagery register before moving on.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading discussion anchors the text in students' own experience of communication before they meet Khetaram's world. A common tendency is to stay abstract; push students to name specific means — WhatsApp, courier, hand-carried notes — so the contrast with the Thar desert context lands concretely. The vocabulary fill-in task (p.204) is set for self-study: students read the six words in the box and complete the passage before the next sitting.

periods.activity_title: Mapping Khetaram — Comprehension and Close Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.207): identity-card information sheet — position, employer, address, transport, responsibilities
Check Your Understanding (p.207): teacher-led discussion — why Khetaram took the job, how he might feel daily

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites a brief oral recap of what students read in the first sitting — Khetaram's posting, the distances he covers, and the desert conditions — to settle the class into the text before new tasks.

Students work individually on the identity-card information sheet (Check Your Understanding, p.207), filling in Khetaram's position, employer, official address, mode of transport, and four key responsibilities directly from the text. Teacher circulates and guides those who conflate 'mode of transport' with walking distance.

Teacher-led discussion on the two oral prompts (p.207): why Khetaram took this challenging job, and how he might feel about repeating it every day. Students are encouraged to use evidence from the prose — the bajra crop, the family of five, the welcome on every threshold — rather than speculation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about Khetaram's physical conditions and the GDS system, students are now ready to articulate his situation in structured form. A common error is listing 'cycling' as his mode of transport; the text makes clear the sand is too soft for bicycles — prompt students to reread that sentence. The discussion of motivation should draw out both the economic necessity (one crop of bajra not enough) and the human dignity Khetaram finds in the role.

periods.activity_title: Situations and Reasons — Completing the Table

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.210): situation-reason table — holiday rule, dwelling on thresholds, BSF lift
Reading for Meaning (p.210): why jaggery was offered on news of births or weddings
Reading for Meaning (p.210): how phone lines would help Khetaram in his job

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud p.207–212 with students following, pausing at the sandstorm description, the jaggery gesture, and the torn-corner envelope ritual. Students annotate any phrase they find striking in the margin.

Students complete the situation-reason table (p.210) individually, matching the 50-degree holiday rule, Khetaram dwelling on any threshold, and the BSF giving him a lift with their reasons from the text. Pairs compare and resolve differences.

Teacher takes up the two short-answer questions — jaggery on auspicious news and how phone lines would transform Khetaram's role — as a whole-class oral discussion, inviting students to quote the text. Teacher connects the jaggery detail to the broader theme of Khetaram's social embeddedness in the desert community.

periods.teacher_notes: The situation-reason table requires careful rereading of the embedded explanations in the prose; students often supply reasons from common sense rather than the text. The question about phone lines links to Khetaram's own words 'Main tayyar hoon' and his vision of becoming a Gramin Sanchar Sewak — draw students to that closing moment as evidence. The unanchored vocabulary fill-in task (p.204) may be reviewed informally if students bring completed work.

periods.activity_title: Extract Analysis — Famine, Philosophy, and Character

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.211): Extract 1 — akaal passage, five sub-questions on famine, survival, and money orders
Critical Reflection (p.211–212): Extract 2 — torn-corner envelope, five sub-questions on philosophy and temperament

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 (the akaal passage, p.211) aloud slowly, then asks students to read it silently once more before attempting the questions.

Students work through all five sub-questions under Extract 1 — the bajra sentence completion, why famine is 'a way of life', Khetaram's reason for working, the analogy completion, and what 'a good year' means — writing answers individually. Teacher circulates, prompting students who conflate 'a good year' with abundant harvest to reread Khetaram's exact words.

Teacher reads Extract 2 (the torn-corner envelope, p.211–212) aloud. Students work through all five sub-questions — the MCQ on who tore the corner, the sentence completion on reading twice, Khetaram's philosophy and action, the true-or-false on his beliefs matching his action, and the aspect of temperament revealed. Answers are shared and discussed as a class, with the teacher drawing out what the ritual reveals about Khetaram's compassion and his view that bad news must not enter a house.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged with Khetaram's working conditions and community role across earlier sittings, students are now ready to read the two extracts analytically. The analogy completion — 'Other families: Money orders :: Khetaram: ___' — trips many students; guide them to see that other families depend on money orders while Khetaram depends on his postal salary. The true-or-false on beliefs versus action is the sharpest item: Khetaram's belief that bad news must be destroyed is precisely what his action of tearing the letter enacts, so the statement is false — his action aligns with his belief.

periods.activity_title: Evaluating the GDS — Extended Analytical Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.212): five extended-answer questions — GDS invaluable, India Post vs British system, trust, Khetaram post-60, author's tribute

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the key distinctions established in the prose — the British dak serving administrative centres versus post-independence India Post's mandate to reach every citizen — to prime students for the comparison question. Students identify two pieces of textual evidence for trust in GDS before writing begins.

Students work individually on all five questions: justifying the Postmaster-General's claim that GDS is 'invaluable', comparing India Post's purpose with the British postal system, supporting the trust statement with two textual instances, inferring why Khetaram was grateful to continue past 60, and explaining the author's tribute. Teacher circulates, nudging students toward textual evidence rather than opinion.

Teacher-led whole-class share: one student reads their answer to the tribute question aloud; teacher highlights the strongest textual anchors — Khetaram as 'an integral thread in India's social fabric' — and draws out why the author frames postal workers in those terms.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write that GDS is invaluable because 'they work hard' — push them to use the specific textual evidence: 1.5 lakh post offices by independence's legacy, coverage of Ladakh, Lakshadweep and the northeast, and the village communities' rejection of patwaris in favour of familiar postmen. The inference on Khetaram continuing past 60 should be grounded in the economic necessity stated — one bajra crop insufficient — rather than abstract loyalty. The unanchored tasks from earlier (p.204 fill-in) may be flagged as independent revision material.

periods.activity_title: Desert Phrases, Literary Devices, and Contextual Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.212): match four desert phrases to meanings, then use each in an original sentence
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.212): identify alliteration and metaphor in the khaki-turban extract
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.213): match five context-words to meanings, then use each in an original sentence

time_bands.activity: Students match the four phrases from p.212 — 'crumbles into sand', 'give a new lease of life', 'turn into a trickle before drying out', 'bearing words across this desolate geography' — to their meanings, then compose one original sentence each. Pairs compare sentences and refine for precision.

Teacher reads the khaki-turban extract aloud and asks students to identify, in writing, one example each of alliteration and metaphor. Class discusses: alliteration in 'scorching summer' or 'swirling sandstorms'; metaphor in 'walking sandman'. Teacher explains how the literary devices amplify the harshness of Khetaram's conditions.

Students match the five context-words — arid, concessional, gaunt, remote, desolate — to their contextual meanings (p.213), then write one sentence each using the word as it functions in the chapter. Teacher draws attention to how these words collectively paint the geography of Khetaram's route.

periods.teacher_notes: The phrase 'give a new lease of life' is idiomatically opaque for many students — ground it in the text by asking what 'new life' the postal salary gave Khetaram's family. For the literary devices task, students sometimes confuse alliteration with rhyme; clarify that alliteration is repetition of the initial consonant sound, pointing to 'scorching/summer' and 'swirling/sandstorms' as examples from the same sentence. The present-perfect and passive-voice grammar tasks (p.213–215) are set for the dedicated grammar unit.

periods.activity_title: Present Perfect and Passive Voice in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.213–214): present-perfect tense — match seven sentences to functions, fill blanks in postage-stamp paragraph
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.215): active-to-passive conversion — fill blanks A–E in Khetaram's advice paragraph

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the seven model sentences from p.213–214 on the board and walks through each function of the present perfect — finished actions, recently completed, life experiences, accomplishment, change over time, multiple actions, past action with present impact. Students then match each sentence to its function individually, followed by a quick class check.

Students fill in the five blanks in the postage-stamp paragraph (p.214) using the present perfect form of the bracketed verbs. Teacher circulates, addressing the common error of using simple past ('I got') in place of present perfect ('I have just got').

Teacher works through two model sentences showing active and passive voice transformation, then students fill in blanks A–E in the Khetaram-advising-nephew paragraph (p.215), converting the active sentences to passive. Answers are checked orally, with teacher attention to the agent-phrase ('by some of the villagers').

periods.teacher_notes: The present-perfect section is rich; the matching task identifies seven distinct functions, and students who conflate 'recently completed' with 'finished action' need a concrete example from the text — 'Khetaram has served this route for fifteen years' illustrates continuous past action with present impact. For the passive-voice task, students sometimes omit 'be' — 'Words written neatly' instead of 'Words are to be written neatly'; model the full auxiliary structure before they attempt the blanks independently.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.215): first listen — fill blank with suitable word from brackets (suggestion/request/advice)
Listen and Respond (p.215–216): second listen — five MCQ questions on occasion, India Post, letter writing, carnival activities, postal department role

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the listening context: students will hear a school student announce an event connected to India Post. They should listen for the type of ending the speaker uses and be ready to choose from three options.

Teacher reads Bhavna's announcement (transcript, p.272) aloud at a measured pace. Students listen and fill in the single blank — whether she concluded with a suggestion, request, or advice. Teacher reads a second time; students confirm their answer and the class checks together.

Teacher reads the announcement a third time at a slightly faster pace, simulating natural speech. Students choose the correct option for each of the five MCQ questions — the occasion, India Post's network claim, why letter writing is being revived, carnival activities, and the postal department's contribution.

Answers are discussed as a class. Teacher draws attention to the distinction between 'interactive demonstrations' and 'theatre and dance' as separate features of the carnival, and asks students to reflect on why a school might mark Indian Postal Day — connecting back to Khetaram's role described in the prose.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'request' and 'suggestion' in the first task; point out that Bhavna says 'I request all students to actively participate' — the verb 'request' is itself the answer key. For the MCQ on carnival activities, 'calligraphy and graphology' is the correct pair; 'origami and designing' swaps 'stamp collecting' for 'designing', which does not appear in the announcement — model close listening by replaying the relevant sentence. The transcript is on p.272 of the appendix.

periods.activity_title: The Great Postal Debate — Who Matters Most?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.215): group role-play debate — postcard vs inland letter vs envelope vs money order form, with verbal cues

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the activity: groups of four each take one postal form — postcard, inland letter, envelope, money order — and prepare their argument for why their form is the most important, using the five discussion points (utility, cost effectiveness, privacy, writing space, enclosures) and the verbal cues on p.215.

Groups debate in character, with each member speaking at least twice and responding to at least one argument from another form. Teacher circulates, prompting quieter students with the verbal cue starters — 'It seems to me that…' or 'That's one way to look at it but…' — to scaffold entry into the discussion.

Two groups share their debate with the class, with other students listening for the strongest argument made. After each mini-performance, the class votes on which form made the most persuasive case and explains their vote in one sentence.

Teacher closes by connecting the money order's role back to the prose — Khetaram carries money orders that are lifelines for desert families — reinforcing why the form is not merely a piece of paper but a carrier of survival.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task asks students to argue for an assigned position, not their personal preference — remind them this is a structured role debate and that the strongest arguments are grounded in the prose's evidence (the money order's centrality to rural life, Mulk Raj Anand's observation). A frequent weak point is ignoring the counter-argument; model 'That's one way to look at it but…' with a concrete example before groups begin. Groups that finish early may be asked to switch roles.

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Condolence Message — Form, Tone, and Completion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.212): draft a condolence message on behalf of parents to an aunt on her father's passing

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly discusses what a condolence message does: it acknowledges loss, expresses sympathy, and offers support. Students read the model message (Sawant Singh to cousin) in the textbook, noting the tone, opening line, expression of shared grief, and closing thought.

Students plan and draft their own condolence message — written on behalf of their parents to an aunt on the recent passing of her father. Teacher circulates, prompting appropriate formal register, correct salutation, and a closing that offers comfort rather than detail about the deceased.

Pairs exchange drafts and give one piece of feedback: one thing that works in tone and one suggestion for improvement. Writers revise their draft based on the feedback, producing a clean final version in their notebooks.

Two or three students read their final condolence messages aloud. Teacher provides brief evaluative comments on register, empathy, and form — connecting back to Khetaram, who reads death notices aloud and understood the weight of such words better than anyone.

periods.teacher_notes: Students tend to over-explain the death or offer unsolicited advice; the model in the textbook keeps the message brief and emotionally restrained — use it as the benchmark for tone. The writing, peer response, and revision cycle is completed within this sitting so no physical artefact carries over. The unanchored philately and telegram tasks from Beyond the Text are flagged as independent exploration for curious students.

periods.activity_title: Daakroom and Philately — Exploring Postal Heritage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.216): read about the Daakroom carnival; discuss its purpose and design as a digital detox
Learning Beyond the Text (p.216): philately — study postage stamps, discuss depictions, group-research five categories, build class-board content

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Daakroom carnival (p.216): students read the short passage about its Ministry of Culture context and discuss in pairs — why would a digital-age government want to revive letter writing, and what does the name 'Daakroom' signal? One pair shares their view with the class.

Students work in groups of five on the philately task (p.216): they study the postage stamps shown, discuss who or what each depicts, and then divide the five research categories — personalities, celebrations, centenaries, nature, heritage — one per group member. Each student writes four to five sentences of findings on their category that could feature on a class board titled 'Philately–Upholding Our Heritage'.

Groups share one highlight from each category. Teacher closes by connecting philately to the prose's celebration of India Post's history — stamps, like Khetaram's mailbag, are carriers of the nation's story — and invites students to find one stamp at home that interests them as a personal follow-up.

periods.teacher_notes: The philately task is open-ended; without research tools in the classroom, guide students to work from the stamps printed in the textbook and general knowledge rather than expecting internet access. The class-board content is drafted in notebooks during this sitting — it is a writing exercise, not a physical board construction, so no carry-over artefact is created. The telegram task (p.216) is flagged as independent enrichment for students who complete the philately writing early.

periods.activity_title: Telegram Craft and Postal Heritage Project

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.216): telegram form — study the form, understand word-based pricing, compose an original telegram for an appropriate occasion

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the history of the telegram — once the fastest written communication, priced per word, requiring extreme precision — and reads aloud the description of the inland telegram form from p.216. Students discuss in pairs: what occasions demanded a telegram, and how word-economy changed the language used.

Students study the inland telegram form (p.216) and compose their own original telegram for a chosen occasion — a birth announcement, a wedding greeting, a condolence, or an urgent family message. They count words, cross out unnecessary ones, and refine until the message is as concise as possible without losing meaning.

Students read their telegrams aloud; classmates guess the occasion and comment on whether any further words could be cut. Teacher closes by drawing together the chapter's arc — from Bhavna's Daakroom carnival to Khetaram crossing the dunes — noting that every form of postal communication, however different in speed and cost, rests on the same human need to carry words across distance.

periods.teacher_notes: The telegram exercise rewards the secondary skill of writing for a specific constraint — word-count economy — which is distinct from the condolence message's tonal demands. The condolence message overlaps the telegram in occasion but diverges sharply in register and length; that contrast is pedagogically valuable and worth naming aloud. The telegram task stands entirely alone: students need only the textbook page and a pencil to compose, so no prior sitting's output is required.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, social context, and authorial purpose by close-reading a prose narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Khetaram's desert postal duty, economic necessity, community trust, and ritual of the torn-corner death notice.
items.item_stem: Which of the following best explains why Khetaram continues his postal route even when temperatures unofficially cross 50 degrees Celsius?

options.label: A
options.text: He enjoys the social visits and cups of tea offered at each hamlet.

options.label: B
options.text: He hopes to be promoted to Gramin Sanchar Sewak before the monsoon.

options.label: C
options.text: He is contractually required to complete deliveries regardless of weather conditions.

options.label: D
options.text: The salary is essential because one crop of bajra cannot feed his family of five.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has noted the social warmth extended to Khetaram but misidentifies enjoyment as motivation rather than economic compulsion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student infers a formal contractual obligation; the text grounds the motivation in survival need, not contract terms.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has recalled Khetaram's aspiration to become Gramin Sanchar Sewak but conflates a future hope with his present reason for working.

items.source_context: Khetaram's desert postal duty, economic necessity, community trust, and ritual of the torn-corner death notice.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage above and answer the questions below.

1. What does Khetaram's ritual of standing outside and reading the death notice twice before tearing it reveal about his understanding of his role in the community?
2. The author describes people like Khetaram as 'integral threads in India's social fabric.' Analyse what this metaphor suggests about the relationship between postal workers and the communities they serve.
items.visual_stimulus:
From the chapter (p.209):
“There is one letter delivery he dreads. The envelope with the right corner torn off, which signifies that the missive bears news of death. "Ashubh Samachar cannot be carried into the house," says Khetaram. So, he stands outside, reads out the letter twice, then tears it to bits. "Bad news must be destroyed," he mutters philosophically.”

expected_elements: Khetaram acts as a protective intermediary, shielding the household from the physical presence of bad news.
Reading aloud twice suggests care for accuracy and respect for the gravity of the news.
Tearing the letter enacts his belief that bad news must not linger — action aligns with philosophy.
'Integral threads' implies postal workers are woven into community life, not peripheral to it.
The metaphor suggests that removing Khetaram would unravel something essential in the social fabric.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening comprehension by identifying key details and drawing inferences from an oral announcement using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Bhavna's school announcement about Indian Postal Day and the Daakroom letter-writing carnival.
items.item_stem:
Which of the following statements about the Daakroom carnival, as described in Bhavna's announcement, are TRUE? Select all that apply.
(1) The carnival is named after the Hindi word for 'post'.
(2) The event is organised solely by the Ministry of Culture without any school involvement.
(3) Graphology — the study of handwriting — is one of the workshops featured.
(4) The postal department will contribute interactive demonstrations to the event.

options.text: Graphology — the study of handwriting — is one of the workshops featured.
The carnival is named after the Hindi word for 'post'.
The event is organised solely by the Ministry of Culture without any school involvement.
The postal department will contribute interactive demonstrations to the event.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: Bhavna announces that the school itself is organising the carnival, not that the Ministry of Culture is doing so alone — the Ministry conceptualised the Daakroom idea nationally, but the school event is school-led.

items.source_context: Bhavna's school announcement about Indian Postal Day and the Daakroom letter-writing carnival.
items.item_stem: Bhavna states that the Daakroom carnival aims to revive letter writing as 'a forgotten art form.' In two to three sentences, explain what this phrase suggests about how attitudes to letter writing have changed, and give one specific feature of the carnival that reflects this revival goal.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The phrase 'forgotten art form' implies that letter writing was once widely practised and valued but has been displaced — most likely by digital communication — to the point where younger generations no longer engage with it. A feature that directly reflects the revival goal is the letter-writing competition, which gives students an active, creative reason to write by hand.

items.item_stem: Describe, in about one minute, the single most important advantage of the money order form as a means of postal communication, drawing on what you know about how it functions in rural Indian life.

expected_elements: Identifies the money order as a vehicle for transferring money across distances.
Connects it to rural livelihoods — remittances from working relatives to families.
Uses specific evidence or example grounded in the chapter's desert community context.
Speaks clearly for roughly one minute with a recognisable opening and closing.

items.source_context: Role-debate among postcard, inland letter, envelope, and money order form on relative importance.
items.item_stem: A classmate argues: 'In the age of mobile banking and digital transfers, the money order form has become completely irrelevant and should be discontinued.' Do you agree or disagree? Argue your position clearly, acknowledge the counter-argument, and justify your conclusion with at least one reason drawn from communities like Khetaram's.

expected_elements: States a clear position — agree or disagree — at the outset.
Acknowledges the validity of digital banking for connected communities.
Uses the Thar desert context — no phone lines, sand too soft for bicycles — to argue continued relevance.
Gives a logical reason why discontinuation would harm communities beyond connectivity.
Closes with a justified conclusion rather than trailing off.

items.item_stem: A neighbour has just received word that her son, who worked in a distant city, has passed away unexpectedly. Write a brief formal note of sympathy to her on behalf of your family. Your note should be appropriate in tone and no longer than eighty words.

expected_elements: Uses an appropriate formal opening salutation and a respectful closing.
Tone is restrained and empathetic — avoids excessive detail about the death.
Acknowledges the loss directly and offers support or comfort in general terms.
Stays within approximately eighty words without sacrificing coherence.
Written on behalf of the family, not as a personal peer-to-peer note.

items.item_stem: A local community newspaper is running a column on 'Voices That Matter.' Write a letter to the editor (120–150 words) arguing that postal workers in remote areas deserve greater public recognition and institutional support. Use specific details about the challenges of such work to strengthen your argument.

expected_elements: Uses the correct letter-to-editor format: date, editor's address, subject line, salutation, sign-off.
States a clear central argument in the opening paragraph.
Includes specific details — extreme weather, distances, weight of mailbag, emotional burden of death notices.
Proposes at least one concrete form of recognition or support.
Maintains a formal, persuasive register throughout and stays within the word limit.

items.item_stem: Match each word from Column A with its contextual meaning in Column B, as the word is used in the prose about Khetaram's postal route.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| arid | completely empty of life or cheer |
| gaunt | dry and barren, receiving almost no rainfall |
| remote | thin and worn from hardship or exertion |
| desolate | far from towns and difficult to reach |

answer_key.right: dry and barren, receiving almost no rainfall
thin and worn from hardship or exertion
far from towns and difficult to reach
completely empty of life or cheer

items.item_stem:
The sentence below is in the active voice. Rewrite it in the passive voice, keeping the meaning exactly the same.

Active: The postal department has delivered money orders to thousands of desert families for decades.

Write your passive version below. Then, in one sentence, explain what changes when a sentence is converted from active to passive voice.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Passive: Money orders have been delivered to thousands of desert families by the postal department for decades. In a passive sentence, the object of the active verb becomes the subject, and the original subject (the doer) is moved to a 'by' phrase or omitted.

items.source_lo: Student connects a prose text to its cultural and historical context through interdisciplinary exploration using project-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: India's postal heritage explored through the Daakroom carnival, philately, and the precision-driven telegram form.
items.item_stem: The Daakroom carnival was designed to give participants a 'digital detox' through letter writing and postal arts. In a short paragraph (60–80 words), explain what a 'digital detox' means in this context and why an organisation might choose letter writing — rather than another activity — as the method.

expected_elements: Defines 'digital detox' as a deliberate step away from screens and instant communication.
Notes that letter writing is slow, tactile, and intentional — qualities absent from digital messaging.
Connects the carnival's goal to reviving a practice that has cultural and emotional depth.
Shows understanding that the choice of letter writing is purposeful, not arbitrary.

items.source_lo: Student connects a prose text to its cultural and historical context through interdisciplinary exploration using project-work as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: Design a brief project plan (in note form) for a school exhibition titled 'India Post: Then and Now.' Your plan should include at least three sections for the exhibition, name one artefact or source of information each section would display, and explain in one sentence how the exhibition connects to the theme of communities and communication explored in the prose about Khetaram.

expected_elements: Identifies at least three distinct exhibition sections — for example, history of India Post, philately corner, and the GDS workforce.
Names a specific artefact or source for each section — stamps, a telegram form, photographs of postmen.
Shows awareness of how India Post evolved from serving administrative centres to reaching every citizen.
Connects the exhibition theme to Khetaram's role as a human link in remote communities.
Plan is organised and legible, reflecting the project-planning skill, not just content recall.
